strengths: The manuscript addresses a relevant, practically important NLP problem for an under-resourced language and clearly motivates the targeted Hausa character and spacing anomalies. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/b329bee826a64e32a1c71e85fa997fb4/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Aggregating 460,301 sentences and constructing noisy-clean pairs could yield a useful resource, while the comparison of several multilingual and African-focused sequence-to-sequence models provides potentially useful empirical guidance.
The evaluation includes complementary character-, word-, and sequence-level automatic metrics, a copy/noisy-input reference point, an LSTM baseline, and a 500-example native-speaker assessment.
The best reported model substantially improves every automatic metric over the noisy input, including reducing CER from 0.0525 to 0.0172 and WER from 0.3823 to 0.0784.

The paper openly acknowledges important limitations of synthetic noise, restricted error coverage, and the absence of downstream evaluation; qualitative examples also illustrate both successful corrections and harmful generation.
weaknesses: The central real-world effectiveness claim is not adequately validated. Training and testing use the same synthetic corruption process, while the human evaluation also appears to sample this synthetic test set. There is no manually corrected, naturally occurring Hausa benchmark, so the results primarily establish recovery of known synthetic transformations rather than correction of authentic writing anomalies.

The claimed calibration against approximately 10,000 tweets is insufficiently explained and potentially invalid. The paper does not state what two strings define each tweet's Levenshtein distance when no clean tweet references are described. Figure 1 concentrates distances around 0.7–1.0, which is also difficult to reconcile with the synthetic test set's reported CER of 0.0525. Matching a one-dimensional edit-distance distribution would not establish that error types, contexts, or ambiguities are realistic in any case.

The random pair-level split is performed after merging corpora, with no reported exact or near-duplicate removal. Wikipedia, Wikimedia, and other OPUS-derived sources may overlap, allowing substantially similar clean sentences across train and test sets and inflating performance. Split sizes and source-stratified results are also absent.

Reproducibility is inadequate for Findings in the submitted form. Despite claiming public release, the paper provides no dataset, code, or model URL; exact checkpoint identifiers, random seeds, model-selection procedure, LoRA assignment, corruption order and sampling details, substitution distributions, sentence segmentation, language filtering, and deduplication procedures are missing. The paper introduces M2M100-1.2B but reports no result for it, while mT5 appears in the table without being properly specified in the model list.

Baselines and analyses do not isolate the contribution. A rule-based corrector is especially important because the synthetic errors arise from explicit known rules; there is no character-level neural baseline, per-error-type analysis, ablation of noise operations or pretraining, clean-input preservation test, significance analysis, or multiple-seed reporting. The unexplained catastrophic behavior of some large models further makes the comparison hard to interpret.

The human evaluation is under-specified and internally inconsistent: it uses one annotator with no guidelines or agreement analysis; the relationship among 'correct,' 'incorrect but meaning preserved,' and 'worse' categories is unclear; and 57 cases are reported as 12.5%, although this is neither 57/500 nor 57/358. Calling outputs with remaining hooked-character substitutions correct also appears inconsistent with the task definition.

Several broader claims exceed the evidence. No downstream task shows that correction improves Hausa NLP, no natural-domain evaluation supports transfer to social media, and no experiment supports transferability to other low-resource languages. Licensing also needs clarification because heterogeneous OPUS-derived sources are presented as a single CC-BY-4.0 release.

Overall, this is relevant preliminary work with promising synthetic results, but the missing natural-error benchmark, unclear realism validation, possible split leakage, and incomplete release/reporting prevent a sound and reproducible Findings recommendation. A next-cycle revision could become viable by adding a genuinely annotated natural test set, deduplicated splits, stronger baselines and diagnostics, and complete artifacts.

strengths: The paper addresses an important, clearly NLP-relevant problem for Hausa, a comparatively under-resourced language. The reviewed manuscript is :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/71da8f077f3942b3a8d5798b7f27c00d/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.

The authors assemble a sizable corpus and define several plausible corruption operations, including hooked-character replacement, spacing errors, deletion, duplication, substitution, and transposition.
The comparison spans multiple multilingual and African-focused sequence-to-sequence models, includes an LSTM baseline, and reports complementary character-, word-, and sequence-level metrics.

The appendix supplies noise probabilities, major training hyperparameters, and qualitative examples—including severe model failures—while the limitations section acknowledges the absence of downstream evaluation and the synthetic-to-real gap.
weaknesses: The central validity problem is that training and test examples are generated from clean sentences using the same synthetic corruption process. Strong performance therefore demonstrates recovery from known simulated transformations, not reliable correction of naturally occurring Hausa writing anomalies. No quantitative evaluation on authentic noisy-clean Hausa pairs is provided.

The claimed realism of the synthetic noise is weakly established. Matching a one-dimensional normalized Levenshtein-distance distribution cannot establish that error types, linguistic contexts, or frequencies resemble authentic usage. The construction of the approximately 10,000-tweet comparison data and its clean references is not explained, and Figure 1's distances—concentrated near 0.7–1.0 despite low listed corruption probabilities—are difficult to reconcile with the stated procedure.

The human evaluation does not resolve the synthetic-to-real gap because it appears to assess predictions on the synthetic test data. It uses one annotator, provides no rubric or agreement analysis, and contains internal inconsistencies: 57 is neither 12.5% of 358 nor of 500, and outputs said to contain hooked/plain-character substitutions are simultaneously described as correct according to the reference.

The evaluation lacks essential controls: a rule-based corrector derived from the known corruption rules, modern spelling-correction baselines, error-type ablations, performance on untouched clean text to measure harmful overcorrection, and results broken down by anomaly type. There are also no uncertainty estimates, multiple runs, or significance tests.

Random sentence-level splitting after aggregating closely related sources risks duplicate or near-duplicate leakage. The paper reports neither split sizes nor deduplication, source-disjoint evaluation, contamination checks, or verification that the purportedly clean corpus is actually standardized Hausa.

Reproducibility is inadequate despite claims of public resources and a replicable methodology. The manuscript gives no usable dataset/code/model URL, exact checkpoint identifiers, random seeds, software versions, complete preprocessing details, LSTM specification, or model-specific fine-tuning choices. Some discussed models are missing from the method list, while the stated M2M100-1.2B experiment is absent from the results.

Several conclusions overreach the evidence. The paper claims improved Hausa text quality, implications for downstream applications, and transferability to other low-resource languages, but evaluates neither authentic Hausa input, downstream tasks, nor another language. The main empirical contribution is consequently a standard fine-tuning comparison on a self-generated benchmark.

Presentation and analysis need substantial revision. There are frequent typographical and grammatical errors, questionable or insufficiently supported linguistic statements, unexplained extreme metric disagreements, and little investigation of why some systems produce CER/WER above 1. Overall, important new experiments are needed, but a substantially revised version could plausibly be prepared for a subsequent review cycle.

strengths: Addresses an important and under-resourced NLP problem: orthographic and spacing normalization for Hausa. The task is well motivated and relevant to ACL.

Constructs a comparatively large synthetic parallel corpus and evaluates a useful range of multilingual and African-language-focused sequence-to-sequence models, with M2M100 substantially outperforming the unchanged noisy-input baseline on the synthetic test set.

Uses several complementary automatic metrics and supplements them with native-speaker assessment of 500 outputs. The qualitative examples candidly expose meaningful failure modes, including semantic corruption and mishandling of named entities.
Reports core training and noise hyperparameters, a SacreBLEU signature, computational hardware, explicit limitations, and an intended CC-BY-4.0 dataset release.
The experiments provide credible evidence that pretrained transformers can learn the paper's specified synthetic corruption process.
weaknesses: The central real-world correction claim is not adequately supported. Training and testing both use synthetically corrupted sentences, while no authentic noisy-clean Hausa test set is evaluated. Matching only a marginal normalized-Levenshtein distribution from tweets does not establish that the synthetic errors match real error types, contexts, severities, or frequencies; the construction of that tweet comparison is itself insufficiently explained.

The supposedly clean targets receive little quality validation. OPUS-derived material can contain translation, grammatical, orthographic, and segmentation problems, and some appendix references appear awkward or noisy. Training a normalizer against unverified targets risks teaching undesirable rewrites.

Train-test independence is unclear. The merged corpus is shuffled before splitting, but no deduplication or source-aware splitting is described; Hausa Wikipedia and Wikimedia collections may overlap. Near-duplicate leakage could materially inflate performance.

Evaluation lacks crucial controls: a strong rule-based or lexicon-based baseline for hooked-letter and spacing errors, performance broken down by corruption type and severity, a clean-input test measuring harmful overcorrection, and downstream evaluation. There are also no repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, or significance tests.

The human evaluation is too underspecified to resolve the synthetic-evaluation concern. It uses one annotator, gives no rubric or blinding procedure, and reports confusing categories and arithmetic: 57 hooked-character cases are described as 12.5%, although they are 11.4% of 500 or 15.9% of the 358 correct cases. The status of outputs that differ from the reference but preserve meaning is also unclear.

Some results warrant validation. AfriMBART's high BLEU/METEOR/F1 alongside WER 1.5763 and CER 2.7170 is strikingly inconsistent without length and outlier diagnostics, while the collapse of AfriTEVA-Large is not investigated. Token F1 is not formally defined, and it is unclear how Hausa-appropriate METEOR resources were configured.

Reproducibility remains inadequate despite the appendix. The manuscript provides no accessible dataset, code, or model URL; no exact split sizes, seeds, model checkpoint identifiers, source versions, or detailed preprocessing and sentence-segmentation procedure; and no precise definition of how each noise probability is applied. It also does not identify which models use LoRA versus full fine-tuning.

The method is technically conventional—synthetic character noise followed by standard sequence-to-sequence fine-tuning—and the claimed anomaly analysis is largely an informal taxonomy. The resource could still be valuable, but only after stronger validation and documentation. Overall, the current evidence supports learning synthetic denoising rather than robust correction of naturally occurring Hausa writing, so important but feasible revisions are needed before a Findings recommendation.

strengths: The manuscript addresses a relevant, under-resourced NLP problem and could provide the first substantial benchmark and correction models specifically for Hausa writing anomalies.

The experimental scope is unusually broad: several multilingual and African-language models, copy/LSTM/LLM baselines, an out-of-domain corpus, a 500-example native-speaker assessment, and downstream evaluations are included.
M2M100 performs strongly on the constructed task despite being much smaller than N-ATLaS, suggesting a practically useful modeling direction.
The authors openly report harmful corrections and uneven downstream recovery rather than presenting normalization as uniformly beneficial.

The manuscript is generally organized clearly and provides core training settings, prompts, error examples, and a limitations section. Source reviewed: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/9502b45059f04e09846588da04393485/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.
weaknesses: The central realism claim is not adequately validated. Matching one aggregate normalized-Levenshtein-distance distribution with JS distance 0.14 does not establish that the synthetic data reproduce natural error types, frequencies, contexts, or correlations. The described Twitter analysis compares OOV tokens with lexicon items or other words rather than providing verified noisy-clean pairs, and the noise probabilities are described inconsistently as both randomly selected and empirically derived.

All principal correction results—including the human evaluation and downstream experiments—use synthetic corruptions generated by the same process used for training. There is no manually corrected test set of naturally occurring Hausa errors. Consequently, the evidence supports recovery of the paper's synthetic channel, not the broader claim of correcting real digital Hausa writing anomalies or achieving state of the art.

The human evaluation uses only one annotator, provides no annotation protocol or agreement measurement, and evaluates just the best model on synthetic examples. Its labels are also conceptually unclear: 27% are called incorrect even though their meaning is said to remain largely intact, while 1.4% are separately labeled worse than the input. This does not robustly establish correctness or meaning preservation.

The downstream evidence is weak for the claimed broad benefits. There are no significance tests or paired confidence intervals; several cleaned conditions do not improve over noisy input, and most remain well below original text. Genre results have overlapping variation, while the classifier-training/evaluation setup does not clearly correspond to a realistic deployment scenario. Since the downstream noise is synthetic, these experiments also inherit the unvalidated-noise problem.

Data splitting and leakage control are insufficiently specified. The paper confusingly says that both the validation and training sets contain 5,000 sentences, does not give a complete train/validation/test accounting, and does not report deduplication across overlapping Wikipedia/Wikimedia sources. The MinHash check against AfriBERTa addresses only one possible pretraining overlap and not internal train-test leakage or other evaluated models.

Experimental reporting is not yet reproducible enough. It is unclear which encoder-decoder models use full fine-tuning versus LoRA, model-specific hyperparameters and selection procedures are largely absent, random seeds and multi-run variance are not reported, and prompts/settings for several proprietary-model downstream tests are missing. The manuscript claims public code and data but supplies no precise repository identifier in the reviewed version; provenance and licensing of 'Other Texts' are also underspecified.

Some reported numbers require auditing. AfriMBART simultaneously has relatively high BLEU and extreme WER/CER values (for example, OOD CER 6.423), but the paper neither explains this behavior nor validates the metric implementation. Claims that M2M100 is best are also inconsistent with N-ATLaS leading several in-domain metrics, and the efficiency comparison contains no measured compute, latency, or memory results.

The PDF fails to render several Hausa-specific hooked characters in crucial examples and in the noise definition, leaving blank glyphs. This directly impairs clarity and reproducibility for an orthographic-normalization paper.

A sound and potentially valuable contribution is visible, but establishing it requires a naturally noisy, manually corrected evaluation set; stronger human evaluation; clarified splits and leakage controls; corrected metric/reporting issues; and substantial narrowing or revalidation of the real-world and downstream claims. These are important revisions rather than minor presentation fixes.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and under-resourced NLP problem, and automatic normalization could materially benefit Hausa language technology.

The empirical comparison is broad, covering multiple multilingual and African-focused sequence-to-sequence models, copy and LSTM baselines, a prompted LLM, automatic metrics, and some qualitative error analysis.

The downstream experiments span classification, translation, NER, and question-answering tasks. They consistently compare original, corrupted, and corrected inputs, exposing cases where normalization helps and cases where it fails.

The authors acknowledge meaningful limitations, including semantic corruption, named-entity errors, domain mismatch, and uneven downstream gains. The examples in the appendix are particularly informative.
weaknesses: The central validity problem is that essentially all evaluation inputs are synthetically corrupted. Even the private out-of-domain evaluation and downstream experiments apply the same synthetic noise generator used to create the training data. They therefore demonstrate recovery from the authors' corruption process, not correction of naturally occurring Hausa writing anomalies.

The realism validation is inadequate. Matching a one-dimensional normalized Levenshtein-distance distribution from Twitter with a JS distance of 0.14 does not establish that error types, linguistic contexts, frequencies, or intended corrections are realistic. The lexicon/OOV and DBSCAN procedure cannot reliably distinguish misspellings from names, code-switching, dialectal forms, or legitimate words, and no manually aligned natural noisy-clean test set is provided.

The human evaluation does not repair this gap: it uses only one native speaker, apparently evaluates outputs from synthetic inputs, provides no annotation protocol or agreement measurement, and confusingly alternates between describing evaluation of the best model, M2M100 versus N-ATLaS, and a focus on AfriTeVA. The labels also conflate exact-reference correctness, semantic acceptability, and degradation.

Several claims exceed the evidence. “State-of-the-art” is not meaningful on a newly constructed synthetic benchmark without comparable prior systems; statistical significance is claimed without tests; and broader claims about improving real Hausa text and transferable methodology are unsupported by natural-error evaluation.

The downstream evidence is weakly analyzed. Genre differences overlap substantially under the reported cross-validation variation and receive no paired significance test; the split may leak source/text identity across folds; several instruction-following tasks show no recovery or deterioration after cleaning; and small benchmark subsets are reported without uncertainty or repeated-run analysis.

Reproducibility details are insufficient or inconsistent. The paper says the “validation and training sets” each contain 5,000 sentences despite describing over 400,000 training pairs; corpus sources such as “Other Texts” are underspecified; random seeds, exact splits, noise-generation algorithm, token-F1 implementation, per-model training choices, and complete inference settings are absent. Reliance on changing proprietary GPT and Google systems further limits reproducibility.

A convincing revision needs a manually annotated, independently sampled test set of naturally noisy Hausa text, preferably with multiple annotators; evaluation separated by error type and severity; clearer preservation-versus-correction criteria; rigorous paired statistical testing; and substantially improved documentation of data provenance, licenses, splits, and experimental settings. These are important but plausibly addressable in a new review cycle.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and under-resourced NLP setting. A large Hausa noisy-clean corpus, correction models, and publicly released code/data could be practically valuable to the community.

The empirical scope is unusually broad: several multilingual and Africa-focused architectures are compared against copy, LSTM, and prompted-LLM baselines, using both character/word error measures and generation metrics.

The results consistently identify M2M100 as a strong efficiency-oriented choice: it approaches or exceeds the much larger N-ATLaS model on several metrics, including on translated out-of-domain texts.

The downstream evaluations are useful and appropriately nuanced. Correction improves machine translation and NER over synthetically corrupted input, while the paper also reports limited or negative recovery on tasks such as MGSM rather than hiding those outcomes.

The 500-example human assessment and qualitative error analysis expose meaningful failure modes, including semantic alterations, named-entity corruption, and occasional degradation of already understandable input.
weaknesses: The central realism claim is insufficiently validated. Matching synthetic and Twitter-derived distributions of normalized Levenshtein distance, summarized by a Jensen-Shannon distance of 0.14, does not establish that the synthetic process reproduces actual error types, linguistic contexts, or conditional frequencies. The Twitter procedure itself is underspecified, and out-of-vocabulary tokens are not necessarily misspellings.

All headline correction evaluations—including the nominally out-of-domain evaluation—apply the same synthetic corruption process used for training. The paper therefore demonstrates recovery from its own noise generator, but not reliable correction of naturally occurring Hausa anomalies. Evaluation on manually corrected social-media text is needed for a clear Findings recommendation.

The human evaluation uses only one annotator, provides no agreement estimate, and has ambiguous criteria. In particular, outputs described as correct according to the reference can still contain hooked-character substitutions, while the categories “incorrect” and “worse than input” are not clearly separated. This limits its value as independent evidence of semantic preservation.

Several conclusions are overstated. N-ATLaS, not M2M100, has the strongest overall in-domain automatic results; no efficiency measurements support calling M2M100 the best model; and “state-of-the-art” is not established against an existing natural-noise benchmark. Downstream recovery is partial, sometimes negligible or negative, and statistical significance is not tested.

Reproducibility details remain incomplete: the miscellaneous data sources, Hausa lexicon, sentence segmentation, exact split construction, random seeds, checkpoint identifiers, decoding settings, and which models use LoRA versus full fine-tuning are not fully specified. The statement that validation and training sets each contain 5,000 sentences also conflicts with the reported corpus scale and appears to be a split-description error.

Data provenance and licensing require clarification, especially because the aggregate corpus is declared CC-BY-4.0 despite incorporating multiple sources that may have different or share-alike licenses.

The paper omits substantial spelling-correction and grammatical-error-correction literature, weakening the positioning of its methodological novelty. In addition, the manuscript’s font fails to render the Hausa hooked characters in several central explanations, directly obscuring the phenomenon under study.
